concepts.title: docker logs and Following Container Output
concepts.description: Docker only ever captures a container's stdout and stderr streams by default. Everything docker logs shows, follows, or filters comes from that one captured stream, routed through a configurable logging driver that decides where it ends up and how much of it survives.
learningObjectives: Explain what docker logs shows: the container's captured stdout and stderr, and nothing an application writes anywhere else.
Use docker logs -f, --tail, and --since/--until to inspect a running container's output without drowning in its full history.
Explain what the default json-file logging driver stores, where, and why it can fill a host's disk if left unconfigured.
Configure log rotation with --log-opt max-size and max-file, and explain what each option limits.
Explain where a container's output goes once it is switched to a driver like journald, syslog, or awslogs, and when docker logs can still read it.

sections.heading: stdout/stderr Is the Contract, Not Wherever the App Writes
sections.body:
Docker's logging is narrower than most people assume until docker logs shows nothing for an application they know is running and producing output. The daemon captures two things from a container: whatever its PID 1 process writes to its stdout and stderr file descriptors. That's the whole contract. If an application opens its own file inside the container and writes log lines there with a logging framework's FileHandler, or shells out to a process that writes to a rotating file under /var/log, none of that is stdout or stderr from the daemon's point of view. It's ordinary file I/O landing in the container's writable layer, and docker logs can't see it, not because of a bug or a missing flag, but because it was never set up to look there.

That's why the standard advice for containerized applications is to log to stdout/stderr and let the platform decide what happens to that stream next, rather than have the application manage its own log files, rotation, and shipping. A container is meant to be a single, disposable, observable unit; file-based logging reintroduces host-specific state that's easy to forget about. If a legacy application insists on writing to a file, the common workaround is to symlink that file's path to /dev/stdout inside the image, so the writes still land in the one place Docker actually watches.

sections.heading: docker logs, -f, --tail, and --since/--until
sections.body:
docker logs <container> with no flags dumps the entire captured history for that container from the beginning, which is rarely what you want once a long-running service has been up for days. -f (--follow) keeps the command attached and streams new lines as they're written, like tail -f on a plain file. It's useful for watching a service react to a request in real time, and Ctrl+C ends it without affecting the container, since -f only detaches the log reader.

--tail N limits the initial output to the last N lines before any following begins, which combined with -f (docker logs -f --tail 100) is the most common invocation: show recent context, then keep streaming. --since and --until accept either a relative duration (10m, 2h) or an RFC3339 timestamp, letting you slice out the window around an incident: docker logs --since 2026-08-14T09:00:00 --until 2026-08-14T09:15:00 mycontainer pulls that fifteen-minute window without eyeballing timestamps in a scrollback buffer.

sections.heading: Where the Logs Live: the json-file Driver
sections.body:
By default, Docker uses the json-file logging driver, which writes every captured line as its own small JSON object (the log text, which stream it came from, and a timestamp), appended to a file on the host at /var/lib/docker/containers/<container-id>/<container-id>-json.log. With this driver, docker logs just reads and parses that file back for you; it's a convenience wrapper around data that already exists on the host filesystem, tied to that container.

That matters for two reasons. First, because the file lives on the host and is keyed to the container, it survives docker stop/start like the writable layer does, but is discarded when the container is removed with docker rm. There is no 'keep the logs after removal' switch for the default driver, so anything you need to retain past a container's lifetime belongs in a log pipeline that ships it elsewhere. Second, it's an ordinary file growing with every line the container writes to stdout/stderr, and nothing bounds it unless you do, which is the next section's subject.

sections.heading: The Disk-Filling Footgun: Rotation Isn't Automatic
sections.body:
Left at their defaults, json-file logs have no size cap and no rotation at all. A healthy, chatty service logging a few lines per request can accumulate gigabytes over weeks; a broken service stuck in a crash-restart loop, printing the same stack trace hundreds of times a second, can fill a host's disk in minutes. A full disk on a Docker host affects more than that one container: other containers can't write anything, including their own logs, and the Docker daemon itself can stop working correctly.

The fix is --log-opt max-size and --log-opt max-file, set either per-container at docker run time or as a daemon-wide default in /etc/docker/daemon.json:

```bash
docker run -d --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 myapp
```

max-size caps how large a single log file is allowed to grow before Docker rotates it out and starts a fresh one; max-file caps how many of those rotated files are kept before the oldest is deleted outright. Here that's a ceiling of roughly 30MB of retained log history for this container (3 files x 10MB), no matter how long it runs or how much it logs. Skipping it is the difference between 'logging is on' and 'logging has a bounded cost,' and it's easy to forget because everything works in a short-lived dev container that never accumulates enough log volume to notice.

sections.heading: Switching Log Drivers: Where docker logs Still Works
sections.body:
--log-driver lets you swap json-file for something else: syslog, journald, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, and several others, each shipping the captured stdout/stderr stream to a different destination (the host's syslog daemon, systemd's journal, a Fluentd collector, CloudWatch Logs, and so on). Production setups often choose one of these so log data survives the container being removed, or the host being replaced, which the default json-file driver's host-local file can't offer.

docker logs needs a locally readable copy of the output. json-file, local, and journald support reading natively. For drivers that don't (syslog, gelf, fluentd, awslogs, and others), Docker Engine 20.10 and later keeps a local cache of the same output (dual logging), so docker logs keeps working. If that cache is turned off with --log-opt cache-disabled=true, or on an older engine, docker logs against such a container returns an error along the lines of 'configured logging driver does not support reading'. That isn't a bug; it's an accurate statement that no locally readable copy exists. Either way, the system the driver ships to (journalctl, your syslog viewer, CloudWatch's console, Fluentd's storage backend) is where long-term retention and search live, and where you go once docker logs can't help.

examples.title: Following Logs Live With --tail and -f
examples.code:
$ docker logs --tail 50 -f web
2026-08-14T09:12:03Z [INFO] handling GET /health
2026-08-14T09:12:03Z [INFO] 200 OK in 4ms
# ... stays attached, printing new lines as they're written ...
# Ctrl+C detaches the log reader only -- "web" keeps running untouched

$ docker logs --since 10m web | grep ERROR
examples.explanation: --tail 50 shows only the most recent 50 lines instead of replaying the container's entire captured history, which matters once a container has accumulated thousands of lines you don't care about right now. Combined with -f, it gives you recent context immediately and then streams anything new, the pattern you want while reproducing a bug live. Ctrl+C only stops this docker logs invocation; the container's own process was never aware a log reader was attached. The second command shows --since accepting a relative duration (10m is the last ten minutes) piped into grep, a common way to narrow a large log stream to the lines that matter for the incident you're chasing. (docker logs replays stdout and stderr both; add 2>&1 before the pipe if you want ERROR lines that went to stderr to reach grep.)

examples.title: An App Logging to a File Instead of stdout: Invisible to docker logs
examples.code:
# The app inside this container writes to /var/log/app.log via a FileHandler,
# and never touches stdout at all.
$ docker run -d --name quiet myapp:with-file-logging
$ docker logs quiet
# (nothing -- empty output, even though the app is actively running and logging)

$ docker exec quiet tail -n 5 /var/log/app.log
2026-08-14T09:20:11Z INFO Handling request id=8841
2026-08-14T09:20:11Z INFO Responded 200 in 6ms
examples.explanation: The application isn't broken; it's writing log lines at the expected rate to the expected file. docker logs comes back empty because it only reads captured stdout/stderr, and this app writes to neither. Every line goes into a file in the container's writable layer, where docker logs doesn't look. docker exec confirms the data exists (exec is covered in the next concept). To make docker logs work without rewriting the app's logging code, symlink /var/log/app.log to /dev/stdout inside the image (RUN ln -sf /dev/stdout /var/log/app.log) so the same file-write calls land on the stream Docker watches. Better long-term, configure the logging framework to write to stdout/stderr directly.

examples.title: Rotating json-file Logs to Stop Disk Exhaustion
examples.explanation: The per-container flags cap this container's log retention at 3 files of at most 10MB each: once the active file hits 10MB, Docker rotates it and starts a new one, and once there are more than 3 files, the oldest is deleted. This doesn't change log content or ordering within the retained window; it bounds how much history, and so how much disk, one container's logging can consume. The daemon.json version sets the same behavior as the default for every container that doesn't override it with its own --log-opt flags, the sensible choice for a host running many containers, so forgetting the flags on one doesn't reopen the disk-exhaustion risk. A daemon.json change takes effect only after the daemon restarts, and it applies to containers created afterward; existing containers keep the logging configuration they were created with.

misconceptions.description: docker logs shows everything my application has logged, no matter where inside the container it actually wrote that output.
misconceptions.clarification: docker logs only ever shows captured stdout and stderr. An application that writes to its own log file, pipes output to a separate process, or uses a logging framework configured to write to disk produces output that docker logs can't see, however much of it there is, not because of a missing flag but because Docker never captures anything beyond those two streams. Making that output visible to docker logs requires either changing the application's logging target to stdout/stderr directly, or symlinking its log file's path to /dev/stdout inside the image.
misconceptions.fact: docker logs only ever shows captured stdout and stderr.

misconceptions.description: Docker automatically rotates and caps container log files by default, so a runaway or crash-looping container can't fill up the host's disk with logs.
misconceptions.clarification: The default json-file logging driver has no size limit and no rotation at all unless max-size and max-file are explicitly configured, either per-container via --log-opt at docker run time or as a host-wide default in /etc/docker/daemon.json. Left unconfigured, a container's captured stdout/stderr can grow without bound on the host disk for as long as the container keeps running and producing output, which makes a crash-restart loop printing the same stack trace a disk-exhaustion risk, not just a noisy annoyance.
misconceptions.fact: The default json-file logging driver has no size limit and no rotation at all unless max-size and max-file are explicitly configured, either per-container via --log-opt at docker run time or as a host-wide default in /etc/docker/daemon.json.

exercises.prompt: A container runs an application that exclusively writes its logs to /var/log/service.log using a file-based logging library, and never writes anything to stdout or stderr. What does docker logs show for this container, and why?
exercises.code:
$ docker run -d --name svc myservice:1.0
$ docker logs svc
hints: docker logs only ever reads from one specific pair of sources -- what are they, exactly?
The application is genuinely running and genuinely producing log output somewhere -- the question is whether that somewhere is one of the two sources Docker actually captures.
Writing to a file inside the container lands in the container's own writable layer, not in any stream the daemon watches.
exercises.expectedAnswer: docker logs svc prints nothing: the output is empty even though the application is running and writing log lines to /var/log/service.log. Docker only captures stdout and stderr, and this application writes to neither.
exercises.solutionExplanation: docker logs is a thin read wrapper around whatever the logging driver captured from the container's stdout and stderr; it can't see arbitrary files inside the container's filesystem. This application writes only to /var/log/service.log and never touches stdout or stderr, so there is nothing for the json-file (or any other) driver to capture, and docker logs returns empty output. That isn't an error state or a sign the container is misbehaving. To confirm the app is working you need a different tool, such as docker exec svc tail /var/log/service.log, which reads the file directly.

exercises.prompt: A host is running low on disk space. Investigation shows one specific container, stuck in a restart loop for the past two days, has a json-file log at /var/lib/docker/containers/<id>/<id>-json.log that has grown to over 40GB. The container was started with a plain docker run and no logging-related flags at all. Identify the Docker-side configuration gap and fix it (the application's own crash-loop root cause is a separate, already-tracked issue).
exercises.code:
$ docker run -d --name flaky-worker myworker:2.1
# ... two days later ...
$ du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log
42G   /var/lib/docker/containers/a1b2.../a1b2...-json.log
hints: The default json-file driver has no built-in cap on log file size -- what flags exist specifically to bound it?
The fix here is about limiting the CONSEQUENCE of the crash loop's log volume, not about fixing why the app is crash-looping in the first place.
Consider whether this should be a per-container fix, a host-wide daemon.json default, or both, so this can't recur on a different container later.
exercises.solutionExplanation: flaky-worker was started with no --log-opt flags, so it used the json-file driver's unbounded default: every line of every restart's crash output over two days was appended, with nothing rotated out or capped, which is how one container reached 42GB. The immediate fix is recreating the container with --log-opt max-size and max-file set, which caps this specific container's retained log history going forward (it does not retroactively shrink the already-huge existing file, which needs to be cleaned up separately, typically by removing the old container entirely as shown). The durable fix is setting the same limits as a daemon-wide default in daemon.json, so no future container on this host can repeat the pattern just because nobody remembered to pass --log-opt (the default applies to containers created after the daemon restart). The crash loop itself is a separate bug to chase down in the application, but bounded logging is what keeps a crash loop from becoming a host-wide outage while that root cause is being fixed.

assessments.prompt: A container's application writes detailed request logs to /var/log/access.log using its own file-based logger, and separately prints only startup and fatal-error messages to stdout. What will docker logs show for this container?
options: Only /var/log/access.log, since Docker prioritizes file-based logs as more complete.
Nothing at all, because the application uses a mix of file logging and stdout logging, which Docker doesn't support.
Every line from both /var/log/access.log and stdout, merged in chronological order.
Only the startup and fatal-error messages that were written to stdout -- nothing from /var/log/access.log.
assessments.explanation: docker logs shows only stdout and stderr, so only the startup and fatal-error messages this application writes there will appear. The detailed request logs written to a separate file are invisible to it. The “Every line from both /var/log/access.log and stdout…” option is wrong because Docker never merges arbitrary files into the captured log stream. The “Nothing at all, because the application uses…” option is wrong -- there's no rule against an application splitting its output between a file and stdout; docker logs simply only reflects the stdout/stderr half of that split. The “Only /var/log/access.log, since Docker prioritizes file-based logs…” option inverts the actual behavior and invents a 'more complete' heuristic Docker has no concept of; Docker doesn't look at file logs at all.

assessments.prompt: A container using the default json-file log driver is stopped with `docker stop` and later started again with `docker start`. What happens to its previously captured log history?
options: It's preserved -- the json-file log is tied to the container object and survives stop/start exactly like the writable layer does; only docker rm actually discards it.
It's automatically archived into a separate, compressed file that docker logs can no longer read afterward.
It's discarded the moment the container stops, since only a running container's logs are retained.
It's preserved only if --log-opt max-file=0 was explicitly set at run time.
assessments.explanation: The json-file log lives on the host, keyed to the container object, and behaves like the writable layer with respect to lifecycle: stop/start leaves it intact, and only removing the container with docker rm discards it. The “It's discarded the moment the container stops…” option is wrong -- stopping a container never touches this log data. The “It's automatically archived into a separate, compressed…” option invents an automatic archiving behavior Docker doesn't perform. The “It's preserved only if --log-opt max-file=0…” option is wrong -- max-file=0 isn't a real, meaningful retention setting for this purpose, and log preservation across stop/start doesn't depend on any --log-opt value at all.

assessments.prompt: A container is started with `--log-driver=awslogs --log-opt cache-disabled=true`, shipping its captured output to CloudWatch Logs. What does running `docker logs` against this container result in?
options: An empty but successful result, since awslogs is specifically designed to suppress all local output.
An explicit error indicating the configured logging driver does not support local read-back.
Docker automatically detects the awslogs driver and transparently fetches the output from CloudWatch on your behalf.
The exact same output as if json-file were used, since docker logs works identically regardless of which driver is configured.
assessments.explanation: awslogs doesn't support reading logs back natively. Docker Engine 20.10 and later normally keeps a local cache so docker logs still works, but with cache-disabled=true no locally readable copy is kept, and the command returns an explicit error stating that the driver doesn't support reading. The “The exact same output as if json-file…” option is wrong -- docker logs' usefulness is driver-dependent, not universal. The “An empty but successful result, since awslogs…” option is wrong -- there's no local copy to return, empty or otherwise; the command errors rather than succeeding with nothing. The “Docker automatically detects the awslogs driver…” option is wrong -- Docker performs no such automatic CloudWatch fetch; you'd need to use CloudWatch's own console or API directly.

assessments.prompt: What does `docker logs --tail 100 -f mycontainer` do, specifically?
options: It deletes every line from the log file except the last 100 before displaying what remains.
It shows only the first 100 lines ever logged by the container, then stops.

It shows the most recent 100 lines of already-captured output, then stays attached and streams any new lines as they're written, until Ctrl+C detaches the reader (without affecting the running container).
It restarts the container and then shows only log lines generated after that restart.
assessments.explanation: --tail 100 limits the initial output to the most recent 100 lines rather than the container's entire history, and -f keeps the command attached, streaming new lines live. Ctrl+C only detaches this log-reading command and has no effect on the container. The “It shows only the first 100 lines…” option is wrong -- --tail returns the most recent lines, not the earliest ones. The “It deletes every line from the log…” option is wrong -- docker logs is a read-only operation; it never modifies or truncates the underlying log file. The “It restarts the container and then shows…” option is wrong -- docker logs never restarts anything; it only reads already-captured output and optionally streams new output as it's produced.

assessments.prompt: Explain what the default json-file logging driver does: where the data lives, what happens to it across docker stop/start versus docker rm, and why an operator would deliberately configure log rotation even for an application they consider well-behaved.
assessments.modelAnswer: The json-file driver captures every line a container writes to stdout or stderr and appends it, as a small JSON object carrying the text, the originating stream, and a timestamp, to a file on the host at /var/lib/docker/containers/<container-id>/<container-id>-json.log. docker logs is a convenience command that reads and formats that same file back for you; there's no separate, more authoritative source underneath it. Because this file is tied to the container object rather than the image, it behaves like the container's writable layer with respect to lifecycle: docker stop leaves it untouched, and docker start resumes appending to it, so a container's full log history survives being stopped and restarted any number of times. docker rm, however, discards the container object, including this log file, permanently; there is no flag to keep just the logs. An operator should configure rotation, via --log-opt max-size and max-file (or the equivalent daemon.json defaults), even for an application they trust, because 'well-behaved under normal conditions' isn't the same as 'will never log heavily under some unanticipated condition'. A traffic spike, a misbehaving downstream dependency causing verbose retry logging, or a bug testing didn't catch can make a normally quiet application log far more than expected, and with no cap that volume has an unbounded claim on the host's disk, which can degrade every other container on the host. Rotation limits turn an open-ended risk into a small, known cost, a defensive default worth setting before there's a concrete reason to.

concepts.title: docker exec: Getting a Shell Inside a Running Container
concepts.description: docker exec starts a brand-new process inside a container's existing namespaces; it does not attach to the container's own PID 1. That makes it safe for poking around a live container, and it's also why it can't help once the image has no shell binary to start.
learningObjectives: Explain what docker exec does: start a brand-new process inside the target container's existing namespaces, distinct from attaching to PID 1's own stdio.
Use docker exec -it <container> sh (or bash) to get a working interactive shell, and explain what -i and -t each individually contribute.
Explain why docker exec fails outright on minimal, scratch-based, or distroless images with no shell binary at all, and describe at least one way to debug those images anyway.
Explain why a process started via docker exec is not part of the container's normal lifecycle: it doesn't restart with the container and doesn't count as 'the container's command.'
Debug a scenario where someone mistakenly assumes a fix applied via docker exec will still be present after the container is recreated.

sections.heading: exec Starts a New Process; It Doesn't Attach to the Old One
sections.body:
docker exec <container> <command> tells the Docker daemon to start a new process inside a container's already-running set of namespaces, the same pid, net, mnt, and other namespaces the container's original PID 1 process was placed into when the container started. This is different from docker attach, which connects your terminal directly to the stdin/stdout/stderr of the container's existing PID 1 process, with no new process created at all. Attach lets you watch (and, if PID 1 reads stdin, interact with) the one process that's already there; exec spins up an independent second (or third, or fourth) process that happens to share the same isolated environment.

That distinction is why exec is the practical tool for interactive debugging: you can run a shell inside a container without disturbing the main application process, because the shell is a separate process. Killing the exec'd shell, or exiting it, has no effect on the main application. It isn't a window into that process the way attach's terminal is; it's an independent process sharing the same namespaces.

sections.heading: -it: Why Both Flags Matter for an Interactive Shell
sections.body:
docker exec -it <container> sh is the standard invocation for an interactive shell, and each flag does distinct work. -i (--interactive) keeps stdin open so you can type input to the process; without it, the exec'd shell has no connected input and is useless beyond a single one-shot command. -t (--tty) allocates a pseudo-terminal, which makes the shell behave like a normal terminal session: a proper prompt, working arrow-key history, and correctly rendered interactive tools like less or vim, rather than a raw pipe that looks broken as soon as you try anything beyond simple line input.

```bash
docker exec -it web sh
/ # ls
/ # whoami
root
/ # exit
```

Dropping either flag changes behavior in specific, predictable ways: -t without -i gives you a terminal with no way to send it input; -i without -t works for piping a single command's output but gives a shell that doesn't behave like an interactive session (no prompt, awkward line editing). For an interactive debugging session you almost always want both.

sections.heading: When There's No Shell At All: Minimal, Distroless, and scratch Images
sections.body:
Multi-stage builds, covered in the previous module, routinely produce final images that contain nothing but a compiled binary and maybe a CA certificate bundle -- no shell, no coreutils, sometimes not even a C library. docker exec -it <container> sh against one of those fails immediately:

```bash
$ docker exec -it tiny-service sh
OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process: exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH: unknown
```

This isn't a Docker bug or a missing flag: there is no shell binary in that image for exec to start, and exec can only start something that already exists inside the target container's filesystem. Reaching for bash instead of sh fails the same way if bash isn't there either.

A few options exist for debugging these images without permanently changing them: build and keep a debug variant of the image with a shell and basic tools added (a common pattern is tagging it myapp:2.1-debug, built from the same sources but FROM a base with a shell, specifically for troubleshooting, never deployed to production); or attach a separate, throwaway container into the target's namespaces from the outside, for example docker run --rm -it --pid=container:tiny-service --network=container:tiny-service alpine sh, which gives you a fully-featured shell that can see the target's processes and network namespace without needing the target image itself to contain anything extra; or use newer tooling built for this, such as docker debug (a Docker Desktop feature that requires a paid subscription), which automates roughly the same 'attach a toolbox container' idea behind a single command. None of these modify the running image, which matters, because adding a shell permanently to a production image just to ease debugging gives up much of the size and attack-surface benefit multi-stage builds were adopted for.

sections.heading: exec'd Processes Are Not Part of the Container's Lifecycle
sections.body:
A process started via docker exec is not the container's designated command, is not tracked by any restart policy, and does not survive the container being stopped and restarted. If you exec into a container and start a background process by hand -- say, a one-off script left running in a detached shell session -- that process disappears when the container is stopped and does not come back when it is started again, unlike the container's CMD/ENTRYPOINT process, which the restart policy and lifecycle machinery manage.

That makes exec a fine tool for quick, disposable checks (inspecting a config file, checking an environment variable's runtime value, running a one-off diagnostic query against the database the container talks to) and a poor tool for anything meant to persist. Someone who execs in, starts a second worker process 'temporarily' to relieve load, and walks away has created something that vanishes on the next restart with no record it existed. It's the same durability problem as editing a running container's writable layer and expecting the fix to survive a redeploy: exec'd state and writable-layer edits are both scoped to this container instance's current lifetime.

examples.title: A Basic Interactive Shell Session
examples.code:
$ docker run -d --name web nginx:alpine
$ docker exec -it web sh
# whoami
root
# ps aux
PID   USER     TIME  COMMAND
    1 root      0:00 nginx: master process nginx -g daemon off;
    8 root      0:00 nginx: worker process
   15 root      0:00 sh
# exit
$ docker ps --filter name=web
# web is still Up -- exiting the exec'd shell did not stop the container
examples.explanation: ps aux run from inside the exec'd shell shows the container's original nginx processes (PID 1 and its worker) alongside the shell itself (PID 15 here) -- three separate processes sharing one pid namespace, as the namespaces concept from the first module described. Exiting the shell ends that one process; nginx's master and worker processes keep running, which is why docker ps still reports the container as Up. This is the observable version of 'exec starts a new process, it doesn't attach to the existing one.'

examples.title: exec Failing on a Minimal Image, and a Toolbox Workaround
examples.code:
$ docker exec -it tiny-service sh
OCI runtime exec failed: exec failed: unable to start container process: exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH: unknown

# Attach a fully-featured throwaway container into tiny-service's namespaces instead:
$ docker run --rm -it --pid=container:tiny-service --network=container:tiny-service alpine sh
/ # ps aux   # can see tiny-service's own process(es), because we're sharing its pid namespace
/ # wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/health   # reaches tiny-service's port directly, sharing its net namespace
examples.explanation: The first command fails because tiny-service's image contains no sh binary, a common, deliberate property of distroless or scratch-based final images from multi-stage builds. The second command sidesteps that by starting a new alpine container, which has a shell, and telling Docker to place it in tiny-service's existing pid and network namespaces instead of fresh ones (--pid=container:<name>, --network=container:<name>). From inside that alpine shell, ps aux shows tiny-service's process, and a request to localhost:8080 reaches tiny-service's listening port, because 'localhost' in the toolbox container is the same network namespace tiny-service uses. Neither tiny-service's image nor its running container was modified; the toolbox container is separate and disposable, and --rm cleans it up when you exit.

examples.title: Why an exec'd Background Process Doesn't Survive a Restart
examples.code:
$ docker exec -d worker sh -c "while true; do echo tick; sleep 5; done"
$ docker exec worker ps aux | grep tick
   42 root      0:00 sh -c while true; do echo tick; sleep 5; done

$ docker restart worker
$ docker exec worker ps aux | grep tick
# (nothing -- the manually-started loop is gone; only the container's real CMD process came back)
examples.explanation: docker exec -d starts a detached background process inside worker, here an infinite loop printing 'tick' every five seconds, and it runs, visible in ps aux with its own PID. But it was never registered as part of worker's startup command; it exists because someone asked for it once, in this exec session. docker restart stops and restarts worker's real process (whatever CMD/ENTRYPOINT defined) and only that process. Nothing tells Docker to bring the exec'd loop back, so it's gone after the restart, with no error or warning.

misconceptions.description: docker exec -it <container> bash lets me interact directly with the container's actual running application process (PID 1).
misconceptions.clarification: docker exec always starts a brand-new, independent process inside the container's existing namespaces -- it never attaches to or takes over the container's existing PID 1. The shell you get is a separate process running alongside PID 1, not a window directly into it; exiting or killing that shell has no effect on PID 1 or the container's running state. docker attach is the different command that connects to PID 1's own stdio directly, without creating any new process.
misconceptions.fact: docker exec always starts a brand-new, independent process inside the container's existing namespaces -- it never attaches to or takes over the container's existing PID 1.

misconceptions.description: If a container's image has no shell installed, there's no practical way to debug what's happening inside it.
misconceptions.clarification: A missing shell only rules out docker exec starting one inside that specific image -- it doesn't rule out debugging entirely. Attaching a separate, throwaway container into the target's pid and network namespaces (docker run --pid=container:<name> --network=container:<name> ... sh), building a temporary debug-tagged variant of the image with a shell added, or using purpose-built tooling like docker debug all provide an interactive shell with visibility into the target container, without the target image containing a shell or being modified.
misconceptions.fact: A missing shell only rules out docker exec starting one inside that specific image -- it doesn't rule out debugging entirely.

exercises.prompt: You exec into a running container, start a shell, run a command that crashes the shell process itself (not the container's own application), and the exec session ends. What is the state of the container afterward?
exercises.code:
$ docker exec -it api sh
# kill -9 $$
# (session ends)
$ docker ps --filter name=api
hints: kill -9 $$ inside the exec'd shell targets the shell's own PID -- what process is that, relative to the container's actual main process?
The exec'd shell and the container's PID 1 are two separate processes sharing the same namespaces, not one process wearing two hats.
Compare this to docker attach, where killing the attached session's process WOULD be killing the container's real PID 1.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The container ('api') is still running normally afterward, with STATUS showing Up. Killing the exec'd shell only terminated that one, separate process -- it had no relationship to the container's actual PID 1 process, which was never touched.
exercises.solutionExplanation: kill -9 $$ sends SIGKILL to $$, the current shell's own PID, which is the exec'd shell itself, not the container's original PID 1. Because docker exec starts a new, independent process rather than attaching to the existing one, killing it affects the container's application no more than killing any unrelated process would. docker ps shows api still Up, its CMD/ENTRYPOINT process running as before; the incident was scoped to the throwaway shell created for this debugging session.

exercises.prompt: A teammate execs into a production container, edits a config file by hand to work around a bug, confirms the workaround works, and closes their terminal. During the next scheduled deploy, the orchestrator replaces the container with a fresh one from the same image, and the bug reappears immediately. Explain what happened and what they should have done instead.
exercises.code:
$ docker exec -it api sh
# vi /app/config/settings.json    # manually edits a value, saves, exits
# exit
$ docker exec api cat /app/config/settings.json   # shows the edited value -- "fixed"
# ... next scheduled deploy ...
$ docker ps   # a brand-new "api" container, replacing the old one
$ docker exec api cat /app/config/settings.json   # shows the ORIGINAL, unedited value -- bug is back
hints: The edit happened inside a running container's own writable layer -- what happens to that layer specifically when the container is replaced, not just restarted?
A deploy that 'replaces the container' is not the same operation as docker restart -- think about which one actually discards the writable layer.
The durable fix has to live in something that gets rebuilt and repulled on every deploy -- what artifact is that?
exercises.solutionCode:
# The fix needs to be baked into the image/config source, not applied by hand to a live container:
# e.g. update the actual config file (or template) in version control,
# rebuild the image, and let the normal deploy pipeline ship the corrected file.
$ git commit -am "fix: correct settings.json value that was causing <bug>"
$ docker build -t api:2.5 .
# deploy api:2.5 through the normal pipeline
exercises.solutionExplanation: Editing the file with vi inside the running container writes the change into that container's own writable layer, the same mechanism covered in the images-and-layers concept, just reached via docker exec. A scheduled deploy that replaces the container starts a new container from the same unmodified image with its own empty writable layer, so the config file reverts to whatever the image contains. The edit did work, but only for that one soon-to-be-replaced container instance, not for the image. The durable fix has to change the source that produces the image: correct the config file (or its generating template) in version control, rebuild, and let every future deploy pull the corrected version, the same discipline as the argument against docker commit.

assessments.prompt: What does docker exec -it mycontainer bash actually do?
options: It starts a brand-new bash process inside the container's existing namespaces, running alongside whatever PID 1 already is.
It pauses the container's main process and temporarily replaces it with bash until you exit.
It restarts the container using bash as its new entrypoint.
It attaches your terminal directly to the container's existing PID 1 process, letting you interact with the application itself.
assessments.explanation: Exec creates a new, independent process inside the target container's existing namespaces; it never attaches to, restarts, pauses, or replaces PID 1. The “It attaches your terminal directly…” option describes docker attach, a different command entirely. The “It restarts the container using bash…” option is wrong -- exec does not restart anything or change the container's configured entrypoint; the container's original command keeps running throughout. The “It pauses the container's main process…” option is also wrong and describes behavior Docker doesn't have -- PID 1 is never paused or swapped out by an exec session; it continues running completely independently of whatever the exec'd process is doing.

assessments.prompt: What is the key difference between `docker exec -it mycontainer sh` and `docker attach mycontainer`?
options: exec requires the container to have originally been started with -it, while attach has no such requirement.
attach can only be used on stopped containers, while exec always requires the target container to be running.

exec starts a brand-new, independent process inside the container's existing namespaces, while attach connects your terminal directly to the stdin/stdout/stderr of the container's already-running PID 1 process, with no new process created.
They are functionally identical -- both connect directly to the container's existing PID 1 process.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer draws the distinction: exec spins up a separate process sharing the container's namespaces, safe to kill without affecting PID 1, while attach is a direct terminal connection to PID 1 itself, so disrupting an attach session can affect the real application process. The “They are functionally identical -- both connect…” option is wrong and conflates the two fundamentally different operations. The “attach can only be used on stopped…” option is wrong -- attach also requires a running container (there's no stdio to attach to on a stopped one), and it's exec, not attach, that's typically associated with running containers specifically. The “exec requires the container to have originally…” option is wrong -- neither command's availability depends on how the container was originally started with respect to -it.

assessments.prompt: Someone execs into a running container and manually starts a background diagnostic script with `docker exec -d`. They later run `docker restart` on that container. What happens to the manually-started script?
options: It automatically restarts along with the container, since exec'd processes inherit the container's own restart policy.
It does not come back -- it was never registered as part of the container's actual startup command.
The restart fails with an error until the manually-started process is explicitly stopped first.
Docker pauses the script during the restart and transparently resumes it once the container is back up.
assessments.explanation: A process started via docker exec is never part of the container's tracked lifecycle, so a docker restart brings back only the container's CMD/ENTRYPOINT process, and the manually started script is gone, with nothing recorded that it ever ran. The “It automatically restarts along with the container…” option is wrong -- restart policies apply only to the container's own designated main process, never to anything started separately via exec. The “Docker pauses the script during the restart…” option invents pause/resume behavior Docker has no mechanism for regarding exec'd processes. The “The restart fails with an error until…” option is wrong -- docker restart doesn't check for, or get blocked by, any exec'd processes still running inside the container.

assessments.prompt: Explain why docker exec is a safe, low-risk tool for interactively debugging a live production container, and also explain its real limits -- what it can't do, and what mistakes people make by relying on it for more than quick, disposable inspection.
assessments.modelAnswer: docker exec is low-risk for live debugging because it starts a new, independent process inside the container's running namespaces rather than attaching to or interfering with PID 1. You can run a shell, inspect files, check environment variables, or run one-off diagnostic commands, and none of it can kill or pause the application process, because the exec'd process and PID 1 are two separate processes sharing the same pid/net/mnt namespaces. Closing the exec session, or having it crash, leaves the service running as it was. That safety has limits, though. First, exec can only start something that already exists in the target image's filesystem -- against a minimal, distroless, or scratch-based image with no shell binary at all, exec simply fails outright with an 'executable file not found' error, and debugging such an image requires a different approach entirely, like attaching a separate toolbox container into the target's namespaces from the outside. Second, and more subtly, anything created via exec (a manually started background process, a hand-edited config file, a temporarily installed package) lives within that one container instance's current life: the restart policy doesn't track it, it doesn't come back after a restart the way the container's real command does, and it disappears the moment the container is removed or replaced by a fresh deploy. The common mistake is treating an exec-applied fix as durable: confirming it works and walking away, only to see the same problem on the next deploy, because the fix was never captured anywhere that gets rebuilt and shipped. exec is excellent for quick, disposable inspection; anything meant to persist has to go back into the image's source (the Dockerfile, the application's config, or its code) and be rebuilt.

concepts.title: HEALTHCHECK: Why 'Running' Isn't the Same as 'Working'
concepts.description: docker ps reporting a container as Up only means its PID 1 process is still alive; it says nothing about whether that process is doing its job. The HEALTHCHECK instruction lets an image define its own application-aware probe, giving Docker (and anything orchestrating it) a meaningful notion of 'healthy' versus merely 'running.'
learningObjectives: Explain why a container can show status Up in docker ps and yet be completely unable to serve real traffic, and what gap the HEALTHCHECK instruction closes.
Write a HEALTHCHECK instruction using CMD plus --interval, --timeout, --retries, and --start-period, and explain what each option controls.
Explain the starting, healthy, and unhealthy states and what triggers a transition between them.

Explain how docker compose's depends_on: condition: service_healthy uses HEALTHCHECK to sequence startup between dependent services, and why a plain depends_on without that condition doesn't wait for readiness at all.
Explain why a naively written healthcheck command can produce false positives or false negatives, and design a healthcheck that avoids the most common versions of that mistake.

sections.heading: 'Up' Means the Process Launched, Not That It's Doing Its Job
sections.body:
docker ps's STATUS column, and the underlying container state Docker tracks, reflects one thing by default: whether the container's PID 1 process is still alive. That's a useful signal, but narrower than it sounds. A web server deadlocked on a mutex, an application stuck in an infinite retry loop against a database it can never reach, a process that has exhausted its connection pool and is rejecting every request, or a service that finished startup incorrectly and is serving 500 errors to everything: all of these look the same to Docker's liveness check. The process is still running, so the container is still Up.

The Docker daemon has no built-in concept of what 'working' means for your application, because that's application-specific: only the application (or something that understands it) can answer 'am I ready to serve real traffic right now?' The HEALTHCHECK instruction lets an image supply that answer, turning an opaque 'the process still exists' signal into something closer to 'this application says it's fine.'

sections.heading: The HEALTHCHECK Instruction
sections.body:
HEALTHCHECK is written into the Dockerfile (or overridden at docker run time with --health-cmd and related flags) and names a command to run periodically inside the container's own filesystem and network namespace -- exit code 0 means healthy, exit code 1 means unhealthy:

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 --start-period=15s \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1
```

--interval controls how often the check runs (every 30 seconds here); --timeout caps how long a single check may run before it's counted as a failure, whatever the command would eventually have returned; --retries sets how many consecutive failures are required before the container is marked unhealthy, rather than flipping on the first blip; --start-period, covered in the next section, gives a new container a grace window during which failures don't count toward that retry total. The command itself is application-specific. Hitting an HTTP endpoint that returns 200 only once the application is ready is the common pattern, but it can be any command: a database client running a trivial query, a script checking a file's existence, anything that exits 0 or 1 meaningfully.

sections.heading: Health States and Their Transitions
sections.body:
A container with a HEALTHCHECK defined moves through distinct states, visible via docker ps (which appends (healthy) or (unhealthy) to the status) or via docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.Status}}' <container>. Immediately after starting, a container is starting, and failures during the start-period window don't count toward the retries threshold, which is why start-period exists (covered next). The state becomes healthy as soon as a check succeeds (a success during the start period counts too; the grace window doesn't delay it), and from then on failures count: it stays healthy through isolated failures and flips to unhealthy only once retries consecutive checks have failed. A transient blip, such as a request that times out once under load, doesn't flip a healthy container; only a sustained run of failures does, a deliberate choice to avoid flapping on momentary noise.

```bash
$ docker inspect --format='{{json .State.Health}}' api | jq
{
  "Status": "healthy",
  "FailingStreak": 0,
  "Log": [ { "Start": "...", "End": "...", "ExitCode": 0, "Output": "" } ]
}
```

Docker doesn't restart or kill a container just because it is unhealthy; HEALTHCHECK reports state and enforces no policy on it. Reacting to unhealthy (restarting the container, alerting a human, removing it from a load balancer's rotation) is left to whatever orchestrates the container, which is the next section's subject.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for Orchestration: depends_on and condition: service_healthy
sections.body:
A docker-compose.yml with a plain depends_on: - db only guarantees ordering of container starts -- Compose waits for the db container's process to start, and only then starts the dependent service. It does not wait for the database inside that container to actually be ready to accept connections, which for something like Postgres or MySQL can be several seconds after the container's process starts, particularly on first initialization. A service that connects to its database immediately on startup, with no retry logic of its own, can race this gap and fail its first connection attempt, sometimes crashing outright.

condition: service_healthy closes this gap, provided db has a HEALTHCHECK defined:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
  api:
    image: myapi:1.0
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
```

With this configuration, Compose doesn't start api until db's own HEALTHCHECK reports healthy -- meaning pg_isready has confirmed Postgres is accepting connections, not merely that the container's process launched. A race that works on a fast laptop and fails intermittently in CI or production becomes deterministically sequenced, through the health-check mechanism and without changing api's own connection-retry code (though retry logic in the application remains good practice, as a defense against the database becoming unhealthy again after startup).

sections.heading: Designing a Good Health Check -- and Its Common Failure Modes
sections.body:
A weak health check can be worse than none, because it creates false confidence. Checking only that a port is open can report healthy for a process that accepted the TCP connection but is stuck internally and never responds to a real request: the check passes, but the application isn't working. A better check hits an application-level endpoint that returns success only once the relevant preconditions are met (database connectivity, required caches warmed, critical config loaded), not just 'a socket exists.'

Start-period deserves care. Set too short for a service with a slow startup (a JVM warming up, an application running migrations before it can serve anything), it lets failures during normal startup count toward the unhealthy threshold, potentially flipping the container to unhealthy, and getting it restarted by an orchestrator that reacts to that, in the middle of a normal boot. The opposite mistake is a check that's too ambitious: having a service's healthcheck verify every downstream dependency, not just its own readiness, lets one unrelated downstream blip mark an otherwise functional service unhealthy, triggering restarts or removal from load-balancer rotation for a problem the service had no role in. The principle: a health check should answer 'am I, specifically, ready to do my job right now,' with a start-period matched to this service's real startup time, not a copy-pasted probe from an unrelated service.

examples.title: A Realistic HTTP HEALTHCHECK in a Dockerfile
examples.code:
FROM python:3.11.8-slim-bookworm
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 --start-period=20s \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health', timeout=2)" || exit 1
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
examples.explanation: This uses Python itself, already present in the image, to make an HTTP request to the application's own /health endpoint, rather than assuming a curl binary is installed, a common gotcha, since minimal Python images don't include curl and adding it only for the healthcheck is unnecessary weight when the runtime has an HTTP client. --start-period=20s gives the application 20 seconds after container start before failures count toward the retries threshold, accommodating whatever startup work app.py does (loading models, warming a cache, establishing initial connections). --timeout=3s caps a single hung check and counts it as a failure, rather than waiting indefinitely for a response that may never come.

examples.title: Watching a Container Move Through starting, healthy, and unhealthy
examples.code:
$ docker run -d --name api myapi:1.0
$ docker ps --filter name=api
STATUS: Up 5 seconds (health: starting)

$ sleep 25 && docker ps --filter name=api
STATUS: Up 30 seconds (healthy)

# ... later, the app's database connection breaks internally ...
$ docker ps --filter name=api
STATUS: Up 6 minutes (unhealthy)

$ docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.FailingStreak}}' api
3
examples.explanation: Immediately after starting, the container reports (health: starting): it's within its start-period, and failures in this window count toward nothing. Once the application's /health endpoint starts returning success, the status flips to (healthy). Later, when something breaks internally and enough consecutive checks fail to reach the retries count, the status flips to (unhealthy); FailingStreak: 3 shows how many consecutive checks have failed, matching a --retries=3 configuration. Docker takes no automatic action from this status change. It's information for humans watching docker ps, or for an orchestrator (like Compose's depends_on, or Swarm, which can replace unhealthy tasks) configured to react to it.

examples.title: depends_on Without a Health Condition vs With One
examples.code:
# WITHOUT a health condition -- api can start before db is actually ready to accept connections
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword
  api:
    image: myapi:1.0
    depends_on:
      - db

# WITH a health condition (a separate file, shown for comparison) -- api waits for db's own HEALTHCHECK to report healthy
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpassword
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5
  api:
    image: myapi:1.0
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
examples.explanation: In the first version, depends_on: - db is shorthand for condition: service_started, which only waits for db's container process to launch. Compose starts api the moment that happens, without knowing whether Postgres inside db has finished initializing enough to accept connections, which routinely takes a few extra seconds. In the second version, api's depends_on requires db to reach the healthy state first, which db's healthcheck (pg_isready, a tool built to check Postgres readiness) reports only once connections succeed. This eliminates the 'database container started but isn't ready yet' race without any change to api's code; the sequencing comes from Compose consulting db's health status before starting api.

misconceptions.description: docker ps showing a container as 'Up' means the application inside it is functioning correctly and ready to serve traffic.
misconceptions.clarification: 'Up' only reflects that the container's PID 1 process is still alive -- it says nothing about whether that process is actually doing useful work. A deadlocked process, one stuck in an infinite retry loop, or one failing every request it receives all still show as Up, because the process object itself hasn't exited. Only an explicitly configured HEALTHCHECK, which runs an application-aware probe and reports healthy/unhealthy separately from basic process liveness, can distinguish 'running' from 'actually working.'

misconceptions.description: depends_on in a docker-compose.yml file automatically waits for a dependency to be fully ready before starting the dependent service, with no extra configuration needed.
misconceptions.clarification: A plain depends_on: - servicename only waits for that dependency's container process to start -- it does not wait for whatever that dependency is doing internally to finish initializing. Waiting for readiness requires the dependency to define its own HEALTHCHECK and the dependent service to specify depends_on: <name>: condition: service_healthy explicitly; without both pieces in place, depends_on only sequences container starts, not application-level readiness, leaving a race window a dependent service can hit on startup.
misconceptions.fact: A plain depends_on: - servicename only waits for that dependency's container process to start -- it does not wait for whatever that dependency is doing internally to finish initializing.

exercises.prompt: A container is started with HEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --timeout=2s --retries=3 --start-period=20s CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1. The application takes 12 seconds to finish starting up, during which every health check attempt fails, and then begins passing every check reliably afterward. What health status does the container end up in, and does it ever become unhealthy along the way?
exercises.code:
# t=0s: container starts
# checks at t=5s, t=10s: FAIL (app still starting)
# app finishes starting at t=12s
# checks at t=15s, t=20s, t=25s, ...: PASS
hints: start-period=20s means failures during the FIRST 20 seconds after container start don't count toward the retries threshold at all.
Every failing check in this scenario happens at t=5s and t=10s -- compare those timestamps to the 20-second start-period window.
The container never accumulates 3 CONSECUTIVE counted failures, because none of the failures that occurred were ever counted in the first place.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The container never becomes unhealthy. Both failing checks (at t=5s and t=10s) occur within the 20-second start-period window, so neither counts toward the retries=3 threshold. The first passing check, at t=15s, moves the container from starting to healthy (a success during the start period doesn't have to wait for the window to end), and FailingStreak stays at 0 the whole time.
exercises.solutionExplanation: start-period=20s exempts check failures in the first 20 seconds after the container starts from counting toward the retries total. Both failures here (t=5s, t=10s) fall inside that window, so neither counts. The application passes from t=12s on, and the first passing check at t=15s moves the container from starting to healthy. It never accumulates a counted failure, let alone the 3 consecutive ones retries=3 would require to become unhealthy.

exercises.prompt: A docker-compose.yml starts a database and an API service. On a fast machine it works fine; in CI, the api service intermittently crashes on startup with a database connection error, even though db shows as Up in the compose logs before api starts. Find the gap and fix it.
exercises.code:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
  api:
    image: myapi:1.0
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:secret@db:5432/postgres
hints: depends_on: - db is shorthand for a specific condition -- what does that condition actually wait for, and is it the same thing as 'Postgres is ready to accept connections'?

CI runners are frequently slower/more resource-constrained than a fast laptop -- what real, if brief, initialization window does Postgres go through after its process starts, and would that window plausibly be longer under CI's resource constraints?
Add a healthcheck to db using a Postgres-readiness tool, and change api's depends_on to require that healthy state before starting.
exercises.solutionCode:
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
  api:
    image: myapi:1.0
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:secret@db:5432/postgres
exercises.solutionExplanation: depends_on: - db is shorthand for condition: service_started, which only waits for db's container process to launch. It says nothing about whether Postgres inside has finished initializing and is accepting connections, a step that takes a usually short but real amount of time and can take longer on a slower, more constrained CI runner, which matches the 'works on a fast machine, intermittent in CI' symptom. Adding a healthcheck to db using pg_isready and changing api's dependency to depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy makes Compose wait for that healthcheck to pass before starting api, turning an intermittent timing race into a deterministic startup sequence however fast or slow db initializes on a given run.

assessments.prompt: A container's HEALTHCHECK has --retries=3. Its check has failed twice in a row so far. What is the container's current health status?
options: There is no way to know without also knowing the --interval value.
starting, regardless of how many checks have run, until the container is manually marked healthy once.
unhealthy, because any failures at all immediately flip the status.
healthy, because the failing streak (2) has not yet reached the configured retries threshold (3).
assessments.explanation: A container only transitions to unhealthy once the number of CONSECUTIVE failed checks reaches the configured --retries threshold -- with 2 failures against a threshold of 3, the container is still considered healthy (assuming it was healthy already), and a single subsequent passing check would reset the failing streak to 0 without ever reaching unhealthy. The “unhealthy, because any failures at all immediately…” option is wrong because Docker deliberately does not flip status on the very first failure, specifically to avoid flapping on transient, one-off blips. The “starting, regardless of how many checks have…” option is wrong -- starting only applies during the configured start-period window immediately after container start, not indefinitely, and there's no 'manually mark healthy' mechanism gating that transition. The “There is no way to know without…” option is wrong -- --interval affects how frequently checks run and therefore how quickly a failing streak accumulates over wall-clock time, but it doesn't change how the failing-streak-versus-retries comparison itself works at any given point.

assessments.prompt: What specifically does a HEALTHCHECK's `--start-period` value control?
options: The delay before the container's main process is even started, comparable to a startup sleep.

A grace window immediately after container start during which check failures do not count toward the --retries threshold, letting a service with a slow startup avoid being marked unhealthy for still-legitimate startup time.
The total number of times the healthcheck will ever run before Docker permanently stops checking.
The minimum amount of time a container must run before docker ps will report any status for it at all.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer: start-period exists so that a service with a real, expected startup sequence (loading models, running migrations, warming caches) isn't punished with an unhealthy status for failures that occur purely because it's still legitimately starting up. The “The total number of times the healthcheck…” option is wrong -- start-period doesn't cap the total number of checks ever run; --retries and ongoing --interval checks continue indefinitely afterward. The “The minimum amount of time a container…” option is wrong -- docker ps reports container status (Up, Exited, etc.) regardless of any healthcheck configuration; start-period only affects the health-status portion. The “The delay before the container's main process…” option is wrong -- the container's main process starts immediately as normal; start-period only affects how healthcheck failures are counted afterward, not when the process itself begins running.

assessments.prompt: A service's HEALTHCHECK is written to verify not just its own readiness, but also that a third-party payment API it depends on is currently reachable. What's the problem with this design?
options: A brief, unrelated outage in the third-party API would flip this service to unhealthy even though the service itself is functioning correctly, potentially triggering unnecessary restarts or removal from load-balancer rotation for a problem that isn't this service's own fault.
This design is fine as long as --retries is set to a sufficiently high number.
There is no problem -- a healthcheck should always verify every external dependency a service relies on.
HEALTHCHECK commands are technically incapable of making outbound network calls, so this check would simply always fail regardless of the payment API's actual status.
assessments.explanation: The correct answer identifies the cascading-failure risk: gating a service's health on an unrelated third party's reachability means that third party's problems get attributed to this service, potentially causing unnecessary restarts or rotation removal for a service that's working fine. The “There is no problem -- a healthcheck…” option is wrong: a health check should verify the service's own readiness, not reach out to check unrelated external dependencies. The “HEALTHCHECK commands are technically incapable of making…” option is false -- HEALTHCHECK commands can be any command, including ones that make network calls; that's not a technical limitation here. The “This design is fine as long…” option is wrong -- a higher --retries value only delays how many consecutive failures are needed before flipping unhealthy; it doesn't fix the fundamental problem of coupling this service's health to an unrelated dependency's uptime.

assessments.prompt: A teammate wants to add a HEALTHCHECK to a service and proposes: 'let's just check that the process is still running -- if it crashed, the container would already be Down anyway, so let's check that our main dependency, a third-party payment API, is reachable, since that's the thing that actually breaks.' Explain what's wrong with this specific health check design and propose a better one.
assessments.modelAnswer: The proposal conflates two things a health check could verify, picking the less useful one and adding a harmful one. Checking that the process is 'still running' duplicates what Docker's basic liveness tracking (whether the container is Up) already tells you for free; a crashed process would already show the container as Exited. What a HEALTHCHECK can add is confirming the service is doing its job (serving real requests, having its internal state ready), which process liveness can't distinguish from a hung, deadlocked, or broken-but-running process. Checking a third-party payment API's reachability, on the other hand, is the wrong thing to gate this service's health on: if the payment API has a brief outage or slow response for reasons outside this service's control, the check would flip this service to unhealthy even though it's working and could still serve every request that doesn't involve payments. If the orchestrator reacts to unhealthy by restarting the container or pulling it from a load balancer's rotation, a provider's unrelated blip now disrupts this service's availability, turning a problem that wasn't this service's fault into one that looks like it was. A better health check verifies the service's own readiness: an HTTP endpoint the application serves itself, returning success once its own required state (its database connection, any caches it needs, config loaded) is in place, without probing an external third party. If payment-provider reachability needs monitoring, that belongs in a separate check or alert, not in this container's health status.
